issues.legal_issue: A higher appellate court may not reverse an acquittal merely because it prefers another view of the evidence when the trial court’s view is reasonably possible and the acquittal is not shown to be perverse.
material_facts: The case arose from an appellate court setting aside a trial court acquittal and convicting the accused; the accused challenged that reversal.

The alleged attack occurred at night, involved many assailants, and took place amid factional hostility, while the evidence about lighting and the witnesses’ ability to identify assailants was uncertain.

Police did not record the earliest accounts of injured witnesses or register a case on the basis of the information available at the scene, and the timing and handling of the first recorded account gave rise to suspicion about delay and possible deliberation.
The evidence contained discrepancies and contradictions concerning the incident, the witnesses, and the identification of the accused.
The trial court assessed these weaknesses and acquitted the accused, but the appellate court did not explain why the trial court’s view was perverse or identify compelling grounds for reversing it.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s acquittal was a reasonably possible view of the evidence. The appellate court was not justified in setting it aside; the convictions were set aside and the acquittal restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principles stated in Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, an appellate court has full power to review and reappreciate the evidence in an appeal against acquittal, but the accused has the reinforced presumption of innocence that follows acquittal. If two reasonable conclusions are possible, the view favorable to the accused must be adopted and the acquittal should not be disturbed. Dwarka Dass v. State of Haryana and Bihari Nath Goswami v. Shiv Kumar Singh likewise require proper weight to be given to the trial court’s view and permit reversal where that view is perverse, legally erroneous, or based on wrong appreciation of evidence. The court applied these principles concerning appellate powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and trial_view_reasonably_possible and high_court_lacked_perversity_reasoning and two_views_possible and (identification_evidence_unreliable or earliest_accounts_not_recorded or material_evidentiary_discrepancies)

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding challenged a higher appellate court’s decision to set aside a trial court acquittal and convict the accused.
predicates.trial_view_reasonably_possible: The trial court assessed the evidence and reached a view of the case that could reasonably be drawn from the record.
predicates.high_court_lacked_perversity_reasoning: The higher appellate court reversed the acquittal without explaining why the trial court’s view was perverse or identifying compelling grounds for reversal.
predicates.two_views_possible: The evidence permitted both a conclusion supporting guilt and a reasonable conclusion supporting innocence.
predicates.identification_evidence_unreliable: The circumstances of the incident and the evidence about lighting and the witnesses’ observations left doubt about their ability to identify the assailants and their individual acts.
predicates.earliest_accounts_not_recorded: Police received information from injured witnesses but did not record the earliest accounts or register the case on the basis of that information.
predicates.material_evidentiary_discrepancies: The evidence contained discrepancies and contradictions that undermined the account of the incident.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a conviction entered after an acquittal, the trial court’s reasonably possible view is supported by material evidentiary weaknesses, and the higher appellate court has not shown why that view was perverse despite two reasonable views being available, the acquittal is restored.
